items.title: Show HN: Trichroma, a Platformer of Light
items.description:
Show HN: Hi Hackernews! I just wanted to share a game I've made over a few weeks just as a little side project. Of course it was developed using Agents Engineering. The idea of the game though comes from around 10 years ago, from conversations with my brother: he is an artist and back them he was experimenting with chromatic paintings that looked differently depending on which color of light they were exposed to. A few weeks ago I decided to show my brother what's possible now a days with AI and how we can turn ideas into reality with a fraction of the effort we would have need in the past. The game is a little platformer, meant to be challenging but cute and entertaining, taking inspiration of games like Celeste or Meatboy. Death is part of the game, and light mechanics are introduced over the course of the 63 levels that are available to play. The development was made fully from my phone with Claude Code, but I invested lots of time on play testing it and I've involved several friends to play it to gather feedback and improve it. I'd love to hear your feedback and I hope some of you have fun playing it!

items.title: Show HN: Build a trading bot in 10 seconds
items.description:
Show HN: Hi everyone, Board is a way to create, deploy, and fund a trading bot in 10 seconds. My co-founders and I built Board out of our own necessity. Every time we had a new trading strategy, we would need to manually input it into our broker accounts and monitor the situation ourselves. We looked at all of our trading strategies over the past 3 years and added everything to the board that would be required to rebuild them from scratch. Now, when we have a new strategy, we chat with AI to create the strategy. We review the board to confirm that it matches what we expect, and we deploy it. We don't have to worry about setting up webhooks for signals or keeping it running on our computer locally. The whole system is built on top of tokenized stocks and commodities. You always have access to withdraw your funds.

items.title: Show HN: OpenComputer – an open source alternative to Devin
items.description:
Show HN: Hi HN! Utpal here, I'm one of the founders of OpenComputer. OpenComputer is an open source cloud coding agent for teams that can run in your own cloud account (AWS, GCP, Azure). We run the agent harness and the sandbox on the same durable VM (architecture in the docs [1]). First commit lands in 24s; the alternatives we benchmarked took 53-72s (benchmarks below [2]). Two other choices: - One VM per team, scalable horizontally. Sessions are isolated in git worktrees. - Session files are backed up to a repo after every turn, so any session can resume on another VM. We noticed that past ~640 session-hours a month, one always-on 4 vCPU VM is cheaper than per-session E2B sandboxes, for example. So at scale, this setup would not only be faster than current SOTA coding agents, but also more cost-efficient. Feel free to try via cloud for free [4] or self host. We would love any and all feedback, and happy to answer any questions! Full demo below [3]. [1]: https://docs.opencomputer.dev/getting-started/architecture [2]: https://opencomputer.dev/blog/cloud-agents-as-fast-as-local/ [3]: https://x.com/IgorZIJ/status/2121309785882591711 [4]: https://app.opencomputer.dev

items.title: Show HN: ArkViz – AI generated software architecture diagrams
items.description:
Show HN: Hi HN, I’m Bryant, founder of ArkViz ( https://arkviz.io ). ArkViz is a product to automatically generate architecture diagrams from your codebase using AI. The vision behind ArkViz is to supercharge both AI agents and humans by providing AI agents deeper relational context using structured model diagram formats, and by providing humans with a rich visual representation you can interact with, with features like zooming, panning, search, and show composing files. In this new age of AI, you can generate a structured model diagram from your codebase in seconds, quicker and better than a human. Not only can the generated diagram be a visual documentation tool for humans, AI agents can also benefit from the context of a pre-generated architecture diagram that lives alongside a project’s codebase. This concept has already been proven by context files like CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, ARCHITECTURE.md living in the root of your repository. The differentiator between ARCHITECTURE.md and ArkViz is that ArkViz generates a structured model diagram of the system, while ARCHITECTURE.md is broader in scope and purely text. ArkViz aims to be a supplement to ARCHITECTURE.md to provide deeper understanding like how components are connected, which components live inside other components, which files compose a component. — Why ArkViz? Software engineering teams often create diagrams to aid in the documentation of their software systems. They are incredibly useful for onboarding new engineers and understanding projects. However, they take time to create and maintain, so are often non-existent or out of date. ArkViz automates the creation and maintenance of software architecture diagrams, seamlessly and securely. AI agents thrive when they have high quality context, including for architecture diagrams. However not all diagram formats out there are optimized for AI. A diagram showing connected systems and components can be represented in essentially 3 ways: 1. Unstructured drawing / canvas format (e.g. draw.io, Excalidraw, Figma, LucidChart) - Quick to get started but hard to maintain. - Good for brainstorming and whiteboarding - The format carries no semantic meaning and is basically represented by pixels, shapes, and vectors. Positioning is stored - Passing this to an AI agent as context has questionable value. 2. Structured diagramming formats (e.g. Mermaid, d2lang) - A level of abstraction higher than a 2D drawing canvas - Good for quick isolated diagram, like on GitHub - Represent
Website metadata: Generate beautiful, always up-to-date architecture diagrams of your software projects from all your data sources. Powered by AI.
items.product_description: Generate beautiful, always up-to-date architecture diagrams of your software projects from all your data sources. Powered by AI.

items.title: Show HN: LarpLess, open-source study tracker detecting distractions locally
items.description:
Show HN: I am ashamed to admit that I am one of those students who go to the library and get very little done (a.k.a. larping). It's very easy to get distracted if you have any electronic devices with you, but as a CS major, I can't just switch to pen and paper. That's why I started building this app called LarpLess with the help of a few friends. LarpLess is a macOS/Windows app that checks your screen and camera with local AI to determine what you are studying or if you are distracted. Gives you a focus percentage at the end, with a breakdown of what you did during your session (Math, Physics, etc.) Privacy is a big concern for an app like this, so it is open-source (AGPL 3.0) and uses locally run open-source models. It doesn't connect to the internet unless you want to check for updates or enable the friends feature (Disabled by default. You can make an account, add friends and see their shared study sessions/share your study sessions). For the camera, it uses an object detection model, YOLO11n, to detect if there is a person and/or a phone at 1fps. For the screen, there are 2 options: the one we did first is reading window titles + a VLM on Ollama (default is qwen3-vl:2b), simple but power/RAM hungry. The one my friend added later can run on an average laptop easily. It takes less than a second for a verdict. It scores window titles + OCR text on the screen with MiniLM text embeddings and scores the screenshot with image embeddings using SigLIP 2. SigLIP 2 decides if the user is distracted, and MiniLM decides what they are working on. You can run the classifier-based mode on any modern laptop. If you want to use the VLM mode, you need a good GPU with enough VRAM (3GB+) to hold the model in it. You can try it out by downloading the macOS version from GitHub ( https://github.com/AlperErg/larpless/releases ) or the Windows version from the Microsoft Store ( https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9nrvvphtmr9x ). I found it helpful for studying. I hope that you will as well. I'd appreciate it if you can give it a go and kindly share your thoughts. p.s. My friend, who also works on this with me, posted about it before but without a description and not on Show HN, so I decided to post on Show HN with a good description.
Website metadata: Break down your study session into what you were actually doing. On-device study tracker for Mac and Windows. Screenshots never leave your computer.

items.title: Show HN: Zeus – Claude Code for AI voice agents
items.description:
Show HN: Hi everyone, Alex here - I’m one of the founders of ThunderPhone. We’re excited to announce the launch of Zeus, a platform that makes AI phone calls actually work without extensive hand-tuning! You can see a head-to-head I made of the last version of ThunderPhone vs this one here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YlkIc3L29lo A (somewhat long) summary: When we started building business phone agents in 2024, we kept running into technical problems that ruined calls, caused by the limits of existing architectures. The two biggest issues were that phone agents misheard callers, and disobeyed scripts or responded in weird ways. Both stemmed from the prevailing voice agent architecture - a “three-step” or “cascaded” pipeline: one transcription model turning caller audio into text, one LLM generating a response (and sometimes tool calls) from that text, and a TTS model turning response text into audio. Transcription models aren’t perfect, especially in noisy environments, with unclear callers, in languages other than English, and on short utterances like “yeah”. With the pipeline approach, when caller audio is boiled down to a single “best guess” text transcript, mistakes are often unrecoverable: there’s typically no “top n” best guesses or other audio signal for the LLM to use if the transcript was wrong. That leads the LLM to respond to what the transcription model thought it heard instead of what the caller actually said. The pipeline approach also caused weird responses and poor instruction-following due to the tradeoff between LLM speed and intelligence. Phone calls demand fast responses to feel natural, which is in tension with an LLM’s need to “think” and run inference - often for several seconds - to answer many prompts correctly. With a single LLM in the pipeline, the obvious choice is picking one fast enough to feel responsive, but that comes with an unavoidably high error rate on real calls, frustrating callers and sending calls off the rails. More recently, end-to-end “speech-to-speech” models have won usage alongside three-step pipelines. They’re better at hearing callers correctly (though still not perfect), but they’re even worse at following instructions reliably, which is typically disastrous for business phone calls. Once we understood these problems, we built our own stack to address them. Over the past year and a half, the ThunderPhone stack has largely solved mishearing and misbehaving by combining numerous models on each call. For audio misun

items.title: Show HN: erXos – a microkernel OS in Erlang based on Genera/Plan 9/QNX ideas
items.description: Show HN: What if every Erlang process were an operating-system process? With as much system code and drivers written in Erlang itself. This is something I was pondering for a while, and finally was able to prototype thanks to AI coding agents. erXos is a capability-based microkernel OS in Erlang: drivers, filesystems, and the network stack are all supervised Erlang processes, same as any app. The kernel itself is Fiasco, in C++, slightly modified for erXos needs. This is an OS I wanted for a long time: an Erlang machine where every BEAM process is a process visible to the OS and scheduler, not something bolted on top. You can try it right now with nothing to install: there is an emulator on the website that boots the whole OS in the browser ARM64 emulator. At the rc prompt, try `ps`, `top`, `ping` or `erl` and write any kind of erlang code. There's a Pi 4 SD image and a QEMU image too. The goal is to build an ultra-reliable microkernel OS with hot code loading and both system and BEAM-based isolation. The latter is one thing that would allow you to run millions of processes on the system, something that would be prohibitive on a microkernel alone due to the context switch overhead. Capabilities keep every component least-privileged, supervision keeps the machine running when drivers or subsystems crash, and hot code loading would let you fix a broken driver without reboot. The secondary goal is to keep as much of a UNIX face as possible. Too many novel OSes change things for no particular reason that makes them hard to use. erXos tries to preserve as many existing UNIX/FreeBSD concepts as much as possible to remove the learning curve. What works today: - Boots in the browser/v64, in QEMU, and on a Raspberry Pi 4 from an SD card - A real shell (plan9 rc) with job control, pipes, `ps`, `grep`. It feels like UNIX on the surface - Erlang versions of basic UNIX apps. - Drivers written in Erlang: UART, virtio, SD card, Ethernet (GENET), display - A pure Erlang EROFS filesystem for root images - A TCP/IP stack in Erlang based on FreeBSD network stack and verified for correctness against it - Domains: every app runs as its own address space or Erlang node, isolated from others - Plan 9 namespaces and 9P everywhere; windows are files like RIO and 9P is a file protocol between OS servers - Supervision end to end: if a driver fails, its supervisor resets the device and restarts it I also have 2 demo apps built on app sdk: a full-screen kiosk app with live crypto quotes and cl

items.title: Show HN: Orbital – Everything (known) in Earth orbit, live in 3D, in the browser
items.description:
Show HN: I look up a lot at the sky at night and made this because I wanted to better understand what is up there. Orbital shows all 32,000+ tracked objects at their current positions: about 17,000 working satellites, 2,800 dead ones, 2,200 spent rocket bodies and 10,700 pieces of debris. Each is color coded, can be switched off, and can be "clicked" to follow. For the well-known ones it pulls up a real photo (where available), what it is for, and when it stopped working. There is an animation that shows launch history from 1957 to today. When you first visit, click on the "Watch 1957 → today" button to see the animation. You can also "fly out" to the solar system and see the planets, moons, comets and spacecraft further out there. My orbit data comes from Space-Track. I also pull from CelesTrak to determine which satellites are currently active. It is a static site on GitHub Pages (currently) with no backend, no accounts, and no ads. It also installs as an app and reopens offline. I wrote it with Claude Code doing most of the implementation. I will provide the link to the source if you want it. I would like to hear what you think about it. Specifically, what is confusing on a first visit, and what would make you come back to it. And anything else constructive you would like to share.

items.title: Show HN: Fast deterministic natural language search for OpenStreetMap data
items.description:
Show HN: I want to show you HippoMaps. It is a fully featured map and navigation app built on OpenStreetMap with a custom Overpass API engine for really fast search of POIs, areas and ways. My aim with HippoMaps is to get to a level where I don't need Google Maps anymore. The biggest hurdle IMHO with OSM based apps is the lack of nice and fast search (where GMaps excels at). To get there I started working on a deterministic (as in no LLMs used) parser of queries that translates them to the Overpass QL. Search queries are split into tokens and the algorithm tries to guess "what" you want to search and "where". The former comes from a word list (known brands, sports, OSM tags) and the latter from the geocoder service (Photon). You can get quite creative like "cafes in Zurich by the Limmat", "peaks over 4000 m in Valais", "pharmacies open now in Bern". It's good for discovering hiking trails, e.g. "hiking trails from Arth-Goldau to Rigi Kulm". It knows how to find stuff between two places, next to a place, near a place and so on. You can stack those as well like "bridges over the danube in serbia 50 km from novi sad". Except the search it has almost all of the features you would expect from a map like turn-by-turn navigation (Valhalla) with voice (Piper), public transport navigation in Europe (MOTIS), live traffic (only a few countries so far). The app is GPL-3.0: https://github.com/cdutsov/hippomaps I'm looking forward to feedback on searches that work or don't work for you + overall comments.

items.title: Show HN: Openspot – macOS launcher for disposable tools
items.description:
Show HN: Hi HN! We're Tony, Kolom and Anastasiia, a small team from Ukraine. Today we are open-sourcing Openspot, our research project on using generative UI in day-to-day work. The idea is simple: generate a tool (spot) for your current task using coding agent, and keep it if you like it or remove it after use if you don't. We are using Openspot daily and really enjoying the possibilities it unlocks. Some examples of spots: - caffeinate, which allows the Mac to work with the lid closed - local file and screenshot search in natural language using EmbeddingGemma 2 - draw on screen during calls or before screenshots - AI agents monitoring - AirDrop, but over the network (using iroh) We built it because of two things: 1. Over the past year, we (and almost every designer and engineer we know) have started making small tools using coding agents. But the DX for macOS applications is very frustrating even for coders, and you have to pay for a developer account to share them. 2. And we kind of miss the days of custom Winamp skins and Twitter clients. That's why every part of Openspot is customizable, so anyone can give it their own look and feel. This is a very early stage. The code is MIT-licensed, and the core will remain free forever. We're sticking to macOS 26+ for now (because of Liquid Glass). Ask us anything, or roast it. Any feedback is very appreciated.

items.title: Show HN: Purple Flow – AI-first n8n alternative, 10k+ workflows on 512MB
items.description:
Show HN: Hey all! I ran into a wall with n8n - hard and expensive to scale, limited streaming, heavy MCP is confusing for agents. That scaling was becoming more and more critical as I was beginning to build agentic swarms. So I built my own alternative with Elixir and Beam. Been using it in production for almost 2 months. It connects my agent to multiple databases, sandboxes, and APIs. I've even migrated over my most used n8n workflows without a hiccup. I ran some benchmarks and 10,000 concurrent workflows executed in 3 seconds and cost about 330MB of ram (listed as 512 in the case study). Equivalent workflows in n8n took 2GB of ram to run 100. It's roughly 200x the memory efficiency of the usual Node/Python stacks. And while you don't edit the workflows yourself visually, you can see and manage them through a UI, along with credentials that the agent never sees. The workflows themselves are pure TOML. Not as easy as dragging node connectors. But the idea is that AI creates the flows and you can easily understand them. This isn't a shaky demo. I'm using it as my daily driver to create complex multi-agent personas, run research and info gathering swarms, and whatever else my agent needs to get its job done. (it's built more than 70 so far) I have a live working demo on my website that was built by an agent using Purple Flow to connect to my server. The demo itself lets an agent using Purple Flow access live (Adventure Works) data and generate reports, documents, and slides on demand. My agent and I built it in an afternoon. It runs on a lightweight model (to save money for a public demo) with very few hiccups. - Repo: https://github.com/leetheguy/purple_flow - Discord, benchmarks, and demo links in the repo.
